paragraphs.heading: What motion means
paragraphs.text: In physics, something is in motion when its position changes over time, measured against a reference frame. The idea covers fluids as well as solid objects. If an object's position does not change relative to that frame, it is said to be at rest, or stationary. Motion is written down with vector quantities: displacement pairs a distance with a direction, and velocity pairs a speed with a direction.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to study it
paragraphs.text: Kinematics is the branch of physics that describes how things move without asking what makes them move. Dynamics is the branch that studies forces and how they change motion. Because modern physics holds that no absolute frame of reference exists, Newton's notion of absolute motion cannot be measured. Relative motion is an object's motion described from the frame that travels along with an observer, using relative position and relative velocity.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's three laws
paragraphs.text: First, a body at rest stays at rest and a moving body keeps moving unless an outside force acts on it; this is the law of inertia. Second, force equals the change in momentum per change in time, and for a constant mass F⃗ = ma⃗. Third, when one body pushes on a second, the second pushes back with a force of the same size in the opposite direction, so the first body is pushed backward. These laws were the first accurate mathematical model of bodies orbiting in space, and they put the motion of the heavens and of things on Earth under one explanation.

paragraphs.heading: Where the old rules stop
paragraphs.text: Classical mechanics handles large objects moving far slower than light, from projectiles and machine parts to spacecraft, planets, stars and galaxies, and it gives very accurate results there. Special relativity is the part of mechanics that compares every velocity with the speed of light c. General relativity brings in gravity, using differential geometry to describe a curved universe. At the level of atoms and smaller particles, quantum mechanics takes over, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle means a subatomic particle's location and velocity cannot both be fixed at once.

paragraphs.heading: Motion you cannot feel
paragraphs.text: People are always moving, in many ways that are harder to notice than walking or waving an arm. Large-scale motions escape us for two reasons. Newton's laws, the third above all, stop us feeling the motion of a mass we are attached to, and there is no obvious frame of reference to show us that we are moving. At the smaller scales, on the other hand, these motions are too tiny for our senses to detect.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's ride through space
paragraphs.text: The Milky Way spins around its dense centre, so the Sun travels in a circle inside the galaxy, and the planets and their moons travel with it. Away from the central bulge, stars typically move at 210 to 240 kilometres per second. The galaxy as a whole is thought to move at about 600 kilometres per second relative to nearby galaxies, or about 582 kilometres per second measured against the cosmic microwave background. Spacetime itself is also expanding, a change in the nature of the universe rather than ordinary movement, and Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are all moving away from Earth.
